title: The Pot and the Cauldron
sum: Ben Sira warns his student against getting too close to the rich and powerful. Partnership with a stronger man is like a clay pot knocking against a metal cauldron (13:2). The rich man uses you while you are useful, shames you with his dinners, drains you, and laughs at you afterward (13:4-7). With a man of power, keep a careful middle distance: do not push in, do not stay away, never speak as his equal, and never trust his friendly talk (13:9-13).

The second half is a sharp look at how society treats rich and poor. Like keeps to like, and the rich and the poor are as natural enemies as the wolf and the lamb, the hyena and the dog (13:15-20). When a rich man slips, everyone helps; when a poor man speaks sense, no one listens (13:21-23). Yet wealth is not evil in itself: it is good "if there is no sin in it" (13:24).
readings: Read as survival advice

The chapter is practical wisdom for a young man in a world of patrons and clients. Ben Sira does not tell him to overthrow the system or to flee it, but to see it clearly and keep his freedom and his honor inside it.
Read as social criticism

The same chapter is one of the Bible world's sharpest descriptions of class injustice. The rich "snort with anger" at the wrongs they do (13:3), and the poor are their "pasture" (13:19). Readers from the prophets to James have heard the same protest.

views.C: Catholic Bibles include Sirach among the deuterocanonical books. The Latin text of this chapter is longer than the Greek: it has 32 verses to the Greek's 26, and its 13:18 holds the line of 13:14, "Love God all thy life, and call upon him for thy salvation" (Douay).
views.P: The Church of England's Article VI lists "Jesus the Son of Sirach" among the books the Church reads "for example of life and instruction of manners" but does not "apply them to establish any doctrine." This chapter is moral instruction of that kind, and it agrees closely with Proverbs and Ecclesiastes (Proverbs 19:4; Ecclesiastes 9:16).
views.H: The chapter pictures a society of wealthy patrons, dinners and dependent clients, and a teacher who has watched how it treats the poor. The Hebrew of manuscript A survives for all of it except 13:14 (folio V recto, line 21, to V verso, line 20) and differs from the Greek in many lines.
views.J: Ben Sira's sayings lived on in Jewish memory even though the rabbis did not count the book as Scripture. The Babylonian Talmud quotes a form of 13:15-16, "Every bird nests with its kind, and a human being with one like him," and introduces it as written "in the Writings" (Bava Kamma 92b).

echoes: Proverbs 13:20; Proverbs 14:20; Proverbs 19:4; Proverbs 19:7; Proverbs 22:7; Proverbs 25:6-7; Ecclesiastes 9:15-16; Isaiah 11:6; Luke 14:8-11; 2 Corinthians 6:14-15; James 2:1-7; James 5:1-6

settings.what: Instruction on keeping company with the rich and powerful
settings.by: Ben Sira (Jesus son of Sirach), a scribe and teacher in Jerusalem (50:27)
settings.to: his pupils, the young men he calls "my child" (14:11; 16:24; 18:15)
settings.when: The first lesson of chapters 13-14, on wealth, from the Jerusalem teacher whose book his grandson later translated into Greek (see the prologue)
settings.why: To teach the pupil how to deal with patrons and rulers without being used, shamed or ruined, and to see clearly how society favors the rich over the poor. Knowing that the hearers were pupils who might one day need a powerful man's favor explains the tone: Ben Sira does not attack the rich; he teaches the pupil to keep his distance and his dignity.
settings.readers: The Hebrew of 13:1-26, all but 13:14, survives in Cairo Genizah manuscript A (folio V recto and verso, T-S 12.864), so Jewish copyists in the Middle Ages still had it. The Babylonian Talmud quotes a form of 13:15-16 (Bava Kamma 92b).
views: Taken at its word, 51:23 means Ben Sira taught young men in a "house of instruction," and these chapters are lessons for them. Their warnings about patrons, rulers, banquets and loans suggest pupils who would move among the powerful.
"My child" may be the convention of wisdom writing, as in Proverbs 1:8, and the book may have been written for any reader. 51:23 does not say who the pupils were or what class they came from.

title: Enjoy Your Goods, Then Court Wisdom
sum: The chapter opens with two blessings on the person whose speech and conscience are clean (14:1-2), then paints the miser: a man so grudging that he will not even spend on himself, whose wealth will go to others (14:3-10). Ben Sira's advice is the opposite: as far as your means allow, do yourself good, honor the Lord with offerings, give to friends, enjoy the good days, because death is coming and there is no luxury in Hades (14:11-19).

At 14:20 a new poem begins. The happy man is the one who thinks about Wisdom, tracks her like a hunter, peers through her windows, camps by her house and sets his children in her shade (14:20-27). The poem runs on into chapter 15, where Wisdom comes out to meet him as a mother and a bride.
readings: Read as Ecclesiastes' advice

14:11-19 sounds like Ecclesiastes: life is short, death ends all enjoyment, so take your share now (Ecclesiastes 5:18-19; Ecclesiastes 9:7-10). Ben Sira adds what Ecclesiastes stresses less: give to God and to friends.
Read as a love poem

14:20-27 is a courtship. The student is a lover who cannot keep away from Wisdom's house. The picture prepares for chapter 24 and for the closing poem of the book (51:13-30), where Ben Sira tells of his own search for her.

views.C: Catholic readers have the Latin form of this chapter, where 14:16 reads "justify thy soul" instead of "treat yourself" (Douay; see the variant).
views.H: The Hebrew of manuscript A survives for the whole chapter except 14:7-8 and shows where the Greek translator struggled: the Greek "offerings to the Lord" (14:11) seems to come from reading the Hebrew idiom "as your hand can" as "to God." The leaf simile of 14:18 has a famous parallel in Homer's Iliad (6.146-149).
views.J: The Hebrew of 14:20 uses the verb of Psalm 1:2, "meditate," for thinking on Wisdom, and 15:1 joins Wisdom to the Torah, a joining Ben Sira makes outright in 24:23.

echoes: Proverbs 23:6; Proverbs 27:20; Proverbs 8:34; Ecclesiastes 4:8; Ecclesiastes 5:18-19; Ecclesiastes 9:10; Genesis 2:17; Psalm 1:1-2; Psalm 102:26; Isaiah 40:6-8; Luke 12:16-21; 1 Corinthians 15:32; James 3:2; 1 John 3:21

settings.what: Instruction on the miser and on using one's goods before death
settings.by: Ben Sira (Jesus son of Sirach), a scribe and teacher in Jerusalem (50:27)
settings.to: his pupils, the young men he calls "my child" (14:11; 16:24; 18:15)
settings.when: A lesson that follows the warnings about the rich in chapter 13 with the opposite fault, the miser
settings.why: To free the pupil from both greed and stinginess: wealth is for using well, for oneself, for friends and for God, because life is short and Hades holds no joys.
settings.readers: Manuscript A copies these verses except 14:7-8 (folio V verso, line 20, to VI recto, line 9).

settings.what: Poem on the man who courts Wisdom
settings.by: Ben Sira (Jesus son of Sirach), a scribe and teacher in Jerusalem (50:27)
settings.to: his pupils, the young men he calls "my child" (14:11; 16:24; 18:15)
settings.when: A poem that opens a new section and runs into chapter 15
settings.why: To make the pursuit of Wisdom attractive, as a lover's pursuit, and to tie it to the fear of the Lord and the law (15:1).
settings.readers: Manuscript A copies the whole poem (folio VI recto, lines 9-21), with an extra line at 15:9 written above the line.

title: In the Hand of His Own Choice
sum: The poem on Wisdom ends: whoever fears the Lord and holds fast to the law will win her. She comes to meet him like a mother and a bride, feeds him the bread of understanding, raises him up in the assembly and gives him an everlasting name. Fools, sinners, the proud and liars never reach her (15:1-10).

Then Ben Sira answers an excuse: "Do not say, 'The Lord is the reason I turned away'" (15:11). God hates sin and needs no sinners. From the beginning he made the human being "and left him in the hand of his own choice" (15:14). Fire and water, life and death are set before each person; whatever he chooses will be given him (15:16-17). The Lord sees everything, and he never ordered anyone to sin (15:18-20). This passage became one of the most quoted texts in the long Christian debate on free will.
readings: Read as an answer to fatalism

Ben Sira writes against people who say their sins are God's doing. His answer is the one Moses gave (Deuteronomy 30:15-19): God has put the choice in front of you. The excuse fails because God hates sin and sees all.
Read as a statement about human nature

Later readers asked what kind of freedom 15:14 describes. The Catholic Catechism cites it for the freedom God gave human beings when he created them; Luther read "the hand of his own counsel" as rule over the lower creatures; Calvin read it of humanity as first created, before the fall. See the card below, and the card at Deuteronomy 30 on whether fallen people can choose to turn to God.

views.C: The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes the Second Vatican Council, which cites 15:14: God willed that man should be "left in the hand of his own counsel," so that he might seek his Creator of his own accord; man is "created with free will and is master over his acts" (Catechism 1730). It adds that "Man's freedom is limited and fallible. In fact, man failed. He freely sinned" (Catechism 1739).
views.O: The Orthodox Confession of Dositheus (1672) does not cite this passage, but on the will it teaches that after the fall man did not lose "the nature and power which he had received," so that he is "by nature able to choose and do what is good," while for spiritual good he must be "guided and prevented [preceded] by grace," and "has it in his own power to will, or not to will, to co-operate with grace" (Decree 14).
views.P: This was the first passage Erasmus brought in his defense of free will (1524), as Luther's reply shows. Luther answered that the book might "justly" be rejected, but that even so the passage does not prove what Erasmus claimed (The Bondage of the Will). Calvin called the writer "of doubtful authority" and said the verse describes humanity as created: "what, then, if we, on the other hand, can reply that he has lost it?" What man "now wants is a physician, and not a defender" (Institutes 2.5.18).
views.H: Historians place the passage in a Jewish debate over fate and freedom. Josephus, writing in the late first century AD, describes the parties as they stood in the time of Jonathan the high priest, a few decades after Ben Sira: the Essenes saying fate rules all, the Sadducees that all our actions are in our power, and the Pharisees taking a middle view (Antiquities 13.171-173). Ben Sira stresses human responsibility. The Hebrew of manuscript A has yetser where the Greek has "choice," and adds lines at 15:14, 15:15 and 15:20.
views.J: The Hebrew of 15:14 uses yetser, "inclination," the word later rabbis made central for the inner impulse a person must master. The Mishnah speaks of loving God "with your two inclinations" (Berakhot 9:5), the Talmud of Torah as the antidote to the evil inclination (Kiddushin 30b), and a midrash calls even the evil inclination "very good," since without it no one would build a house or marry (Genesis Rabbah 9:7). Rabbi Akiva's saying, "Everything is foreseen yet freedom of choice is granted" (Mishnah Avot 3:15), holds God's knowledge and human freedom together as Ben Sira does.

deep.b:
Augustine, writing On Grace and Free Will (AD 426-427), quotes 15:11-17 against people who excuse their sins by blaming God, and comments that the passage plainly sets before us "the free choice of the human will" (chapter 3). In the same work he argues at length that the will needs God's grace to do good, so for him the passage proves that sin is our own, not that we can save ourselves.

Eleven centuries later the passage was the first text Erasmus brought in defense of free will, according to Luther's reply: "The first is that taken from Ecclus. xv." Luther answered that "although I might justly reject this book, for the moment I admit it," and then argued that "the hand of his own counsel" means the dominion God gave humans over the creatures (Genesis 1:26), while toward God a person is ruled by God's commands, so that the passage "makes against Freewill, not for it" (The Bondage of the Will, part 3, in E. T. Vaughan's 1823 translation). He added that the "if thou wilt" of 15:15 speaks "not of the first man only, but of any man, and every man," and warns a person of his own weakness. Calvin, in the Institutes (2.5.18), called the author "a writer of doubtful authority" and granted that humans were created upright, but asked, "what, then, if we, on the other hand, can reply that he has lost it?" and said that "what he now wants is a physician, and not a defender." The Catholic Catechism, by contrast, cites 15:14 for the freedom God gave human beings in creating them (1730), and goes on to say that this freedom is "limited and fallible" (1739). The different ways of reading one verse show the different places the churches give to Sirach and to the fall.

deep.h: Yetser: from Ben Sira to the rabbis
deep.b: In Genesis the noun yetser, from the verb "to shape," is what the human heart forms: "every plan their hearts shaped was nothing but evil all day long" (Genesis 6:5), "what the human heart shapes is evil from youth on" (Genesis 8:21). Ben Sira's Hebrew uses the word for the inner power of choosing that God placed in human hands (15:14). It is not evil in itself; it is the capacity that makes the commandments meaningful (15:15). The Hebrew copy also has a second line, "he put him in the hand of his robber," which Hart (1909) explains as a later gloss that already reads the yetser as an evil force. The rabbis spoke of two inclinations, good and evil, and taught that Torah is the remedy for the evil one (Kiddushin 30b). The longer Greek of 17:16, "every person from youth up is bent on evil," shows the darker reading entering the Greek tradition too.

echoes: Deuteronomy 30:15-19; Jeremiah 21:8; Genesis 6:5; Genesis 8:21; Proverbs 9:5; Psalm 50:16; Psalm 33:18; James 1:13-15; Romans 7:19; Romans 9:16; John 6:35; Mishnah Avot 3:15; Kiddushin 30b

settings.what: Disputation: "Do not say that God made me sin"
settings.by: Ben Sira (Jesus son of Sirach), a scribe and teacher in Jerusalem (50:27)
settings.to: his pupils, the young men he calls "my child" (14:11; 16:24; 18:15)
settings.when: A lesson that answers an excuse, set right after the poem on Wisdom
settings.why: To take away the excuse that God is to blame for one's sins, and to set each pupil before the choice of the commandments, as Moses set Israel before life and death (Deuteronomy 30:15-19).
settings.readers: Manuscript A copies the passage with extra lines (folio VI recto, line 22, to VI verso, line 2). Christian readers made it a key text on free will: Augustine quotes 15:11-17 (On Grace and Free Will, chapter 3), Erasmus brought it against Luther, and Luther and Calvin answered it.

traditions.q: Ben Sira says God made the human being "and left him in the hand of his own choice" (15:14). What freedom is the verse speaking of?
views: The freedom God gave human beings in creating them. The Catechism quotes the Second Vatican Council, which cites 15:14: God willed that man be "left in the hand of his own counsel," so that he might seek his Creator of his own accord, and man is "created with free will and is master over his acts" (Catechism 1730). It adds that this freedom is "limited and fallible": man "freely sinned" (Catechism 1739).

Rule over the lower creatures, not a free will toward God. Luther, answering Erasmus, said he "might justly reject this book" but would answer it anyway: "the hand of his own counsel" is the dominion God gave humans over the creatures, while in the things of God a person is led by God's commands, so the passage "makes against Freewill, not for it." The "if thou wilt" speaks "not of the first man only, but of any man, and every man," and warns him of his weakness (The Bondage of the Will, part 3).

The freedom of humanity as first created, which the fall lost. Calvin called the author "a writer of doubtful authority," granted that man received a power to choose at his creation, and asked, "what, then, if we, on the other hand, can reply that he has lost it?" What man "now wants is a physician, and not a defender" (Institutes 2.5.18).

title: God Spared No One, and Sees Everyone
sum: Many children are no blessing without the fear of the Lord; one good person is worth a thousand, and it is better to die childless than to leave ungodly children (16:1-4). Then comes a list of judgments from the past: fire on a gathering of sinners, the giants of old, Sodom, the nations of Canaan, the six hundred thousand who died in the desert (16:6-10). God has both mercy and anger, and he judges everyone by his works (16:11-14). The longer text adds two lines on Pharaoh's hardening and on God's light (16:15-16).

Next Ben Sira answers another excuse: "I can hide from the Lord" (16:17), as if one person could be lost in the crowd. Heaven and earth shake when God comes, and his ways are hidden only from fools (16:18-23). Then he begins a hymn: God set his works in order at creation; the heavens keep their places and never tire; and he filled the earth with living creatures, who return to it (16:24-30).
readings: Read as warning

The list of 16:6-10 is a sermon in miniature: look at history, and see that God punishes the stubborn, even his own people in the wilderness. Its examples recur in Wisdom of Solomon, 3 Maccabees, 2 Peter and Jude.
Read as theology of creation

From 16:24 the tone changes. God's judgments are part of an ordered world: the heavens obey him (16:27-28), and so should people. The hymn continues through 17:14 with the creation of humanity and the covenant.

views.C: In the Latin, 16:15 reads "every mercy shall make a place for every man according to the merit of his works" (Douay), where the Greek 16:14 says simply "according to his works." The Plain follows the Greek. On almsgiving see the card at Tobit 4.
views.H: The Hebrew of manuscript A runs to 16:26 and contains 16:15-16, which Vaticanus lacks and Swete's notes do not record for Sinaiticus or Alexandrinus. In 16:16 the Greek "with adamant" seems to come from a misreading of the Hebrew "to the sons of Adam" (Hart, 1909). The list of 16:6-10 belongs with other lists of past judgments (see the deeper study).
views.J: The Hebrew of manuscript A names "the princes of old" (16:7) and "the nation of the ban" (16:9) where the Greek has the giants and "the nation of destruction."

deep.b: Ben Sira's list (16:6-10) has close cousins. Wisdom of Solomon recalls the "proud giants" of the flood (Wisdom of Solomon 14:6); 3 Maccabees has a high priest pray, "Giants were among them, sure of their own strength and daring," and "The Sodomites practiced arrogance" (3 Maccabees 2:4-5); 2 Peter lists the angels who sinned, the ancient world and Sodom and Gomorrah (2 Peter 2:4-6); Jude lists the wilderness generation, the angels and Sodom (Jude 5-7). The lists share a purpose: to show that God's patience is not weakness and that judgment falls on pride. Ben Sira's is the shortest and, alone among them, ends with Israel's own ancestors.

echoes: Genesis 6:4; Genesis 19:1-29; Ezekiel 16:49-50; Numbers 11:21; Numbers 14:22-35; Numbers 16:35; Psalm 106:18; Exodus 34:6-7; Exodus 7:3; Psalm 62:12; Romans 2:6; Psalm 139:7-12; 1 Kings 8:27; Psalm 148:6; Psalm 104:29; Wisdom of Solomon 14:6; 3 Maccabees 2:4-5; 2 Peter 2:4-6; Jude 5-7

settings.what: Instruction and warning: children, past judgments, and the sinner who thinks God does not see
settings.by: Ben Sira (Jesus son of Sirach), a scribe and teacher in Jerusalem (50:27)
settings.to: his pupils, the young men he calls "my child" (14:11; 16:24; 18:15)
settings.when: A lesson that follows the disputation on free will (15:11-20) and answers a second excuse (16:17)
settings.why: To warn against trusting in numbers (of children or of allies), and against the comfortable thought that God is too far away to notice one person's sins.
settings.readers: Manuscript A copies the whole section (folio VI verso, lines 2-27), including 16:15-16, which Vaticanus lacks.

settings.by: Ben Sira (Jesus son of Sirach), a scribe and teacher in Jerusalem (50:27)
settings.to: his pupils, the young men he calls "my child" (14:11; 16:24; 18:15)
settings.when: A new section that opens with a call to listen (16:24)
settings.why: To ground the pupil's obedience in the order of the world: God made the heavens obedient, made humans with knowledge and choice, and gave Israel his law and covenant.
settings.readers: Manuscript A ends at 16:26 (folio VI verso, line 29); the rest of the hymn reached later readers in Greek and Latin only. The longer Greek adds lines at 17:5 and 17:9-10.

title: Made from the Earth, Given the Law of Life
sum: Ben Sira retells the making of humanity. The Lord formed the human being from earth and returns him to it; he gave numbered days, power over the creatures, his own image, the senses, a mind and the gift of choice; he showed them good and evil and set his eye on their hearts (17:1-10). Then, without a break, the story moves to Sinai: God gave them knowledge and the law of life, an everlasting covenant; they saw his glory and heard his voice, and he commanded each about his neighbor (17:11-14).

Each nation has its ruler, but Israel is the Lord's own share (17:17). God sees every deed and will repay, but he has opened a road back for those who repent (17:19-24). So Ben Sira calls: turn back to the Lord now, because in Hades no one praises him (17:25-28). How great is his mercy, for humans are not immortal; they are earth and ashes (17:29-32).
readings: Read as a creation psalm
17:1-14 is close to Psalm 8 and Genesis 1-2: humans are small and mortal, yet crowned with gifts and set over the creatures.
Read as covenant theology

The shift from creation to Sinai suggests that for Ben Sira the Law is the goal of creation: God made humans able to choose so that he could give them "the law of life." Paul, by contrast, says the commandment meant for life brought death because of sin (Romans 7:10).

views.C: The Latin text adds and rearranges lines: "secundum imaginem suam fecit illum" stands in 17:1, and 17:5 tells of the making of a "helpmate" like Adam (Genesis 2:18).
views.H: Four verse numbers (17:5, 16, 18, 21) and added lines in 17:9-10, 22, 26 and 29 mark places where the longer Greek text, known from minuscules such as 70, 106 and 248, expanded the book. Some additions bring in ideas not in Vaticanus: a numbered list of human faculties (17:5) and a darker view of human nature (17:16). No Hebrew of this chapter survives in manuscript A, which ends at 16:26.
views.J: "Israel is the Lord's share" (17:17) echoes Deuteronomy 32:8-9, and the rulers of the nations may be the angelic princes of later Jewish thought (Daniel 10:13, 20). The chapter joins creation and Sinai into one story of God's gifts, with the Torah as the last and greatest.

echoes: Genesis 1:26-28; Genesis 2:7; Genesis 3:19; Genesis 9:2; Deuteronomy 5:24; Deuteronomy 30:15-20; Deuteronomy 32:8-10; Exodus 4:22; Leviticus 19:18; Psalm 8:4-8; Psalm 6:5; Psalm 115:17; Isaiah 38:18-19; Hosea 14:1-2; Genesis 18:27; 2 Peter 3:9

settings.what: Teaching on God's sight, judgment and the way back
settings.by: Ben Sira (Jesus son of Sirach), a scribe and teacher in Jerusalem (50:27)
settings.to: his pupils, the young men he calls "my child" (14:11; 16:24; 18:15)
settings.when: Within the hymn's second half, after the giving of the covenant (17:11-14)
settings.why: To assure the pupil that God sees all, that Israel is his own people, and that judgment is real but repentance is always open.
settings.readers: No Hebrew of these verses survives. Later Greek copies (minuscules 70, 106 and 248) added three verses, 17:16, 17:18 and 17:21, with a darker view of human nature and a stronger stress on Israel as God's firstborn.

settings.by: Ben Sira (Jesus son of Sirach), a scribe and teacher in Jerusalem (50:27)
settings.to: his pupils, the young men he calls "my child" (14:11; 16:24; 18:15)
settings.when: The close of the hymn, turning from God's mercy to the pupil's response
settings.why: To urge an immediate return to God, now, while one is alive to praise him; Ben Sira expects no praise from the dead.
settings.readers: No Hebrew of these verses survives. Later Greek copies add a reason to repent at 17:26, "he will lead you out of darkness into the light of health."

title: A Drop in the Sea
sum: A hymn to God's greatness opens the chapter. The one who lives forever made all things; the Lord alone will be proven right; no one can tell his works in full or trace his wonders, and when a person finishes searching he is only beginning (18:1-7). What is a human being? At most a hundred years, a drop in the sea beside eternity. That is why the Lord is patient and pours out mercy, not only on Israel but on all flesh, like a shepherd turning back his flock (18:8-14).

The rest of the chapter is practical: give without hurting words, since a kind word is worth more than a gift (18:15-18); learn before you speak, examine yourself before judgment, pay your vows, remember hard times in good ones (18:19-29). A new section, titled "Self-control" in the manuscripts, warns against appetite, luxury and running up debts for banquets (18:30-33).
readings: Read as a hymn
18:1-14 stands with Psalm 8, Psalm 90 and Psalm 103: human smallness is the reason for God's mercy, not an excuse for despair.
Read as a handbook of prudence
18:15-33 is advice for a careful life: think ahead about speech, health, judgment, vows, money and desire.

views.C: The Latin "creavit omnia simul" (18:1) shaped Augustine's teaching that God created all things at once (The Literal Meaning of Genesis 6.3.4). The Latin of 18:22, "Let nothing hinder thee from praying always" (Douay), differs from the Greek, which speaks of paying a vow.
views.H: The section title "Self-control of the soul" at 18:30 is one of several headings in the Greek manuscripts, which differ on where to put them (Sinaiticus has it before 18:15). The banquet language of 18:32-33 uses the Greek word for a contribution to a shared meal (symbolē), though the Hebrew of manuscript C speaks in the words of Deuteronomy of the glutton and the drunkard.
views.J: The vows of 18:22-23 are those of Deuteronomy 23:21 and Ecclesiastes 5:4-5.

echoes: Ecclesiastes 3:11; Ecclesiastes 3:14; Psalm 8:4; Psalm 90:4; Psalm 90:10; Psalm 103:14; Psalm 144:3; Psalm 145:3; Romans 11:33; 2 Peter 3:8-9; Isaiah 40:11; Proverbs 3:11-12; Hebrews 12:5-6; Proverbs 18:13; James 1:19; 1 Corinthians 11:31; Deuteronomy 23:21; Deuteronomy 6:16; Deuteronomy 21:20; Proverbs 23:20-21; Galatians 5:23; Luke 1:28

settings.what: Hymn on God's greatness and mercy
settings.by: Ben Sira (Jesus son of Sirach), a scribe and teacher in Jerusalem (50:27)
settings.to: his pupils, the young men he calls "my child" (14:11; 16:24; 18:15)
settings.why: To humble the pupil before God's greatness and to comfort him with God's patience toward short-lived humans.
settings.readers: No Hebrew of these verses survives. Augustine quotes 18:1 in its Latin form, "Qui vivit in aeternum, creavit omnia simul" (The Literal Meaning of Genesis 6.3.4).

settings.what: Instruction on giving, prudence and preparation
settings.by: Ben Sira (Jesus son of Sirach), a scribe and teacher in Jerusalem (50:27)
settings.to: his pupils, the young men he calls "my child" (14:11; 16:24; 18:15)
settings.when: A run of practical sayings after the hymn
settings.why: To teach the habits of a careful life: kindness in giving, thought before speech, self-examination, and keeping one's vows.
settings.readers: No Hebrew of these verses survives in the manuscripts read for this page; they reached later readers through the Greek and the Latin, which reads 18:22 as a call to pray always.

settings.by: Ben Sira (Jesus son of Sirach), a scribe and teacher in Jerusalem (50:27)
settings.to: his pupils, the young men he calls "my child" (14:11; 16:24; 18:15)
settings.when: A new section, headed "Self-control of the soul" in Vaticanus
settings.why: To warn a young man against appetite, luxury and the debts that banquets bring.
settings.readers: Cairo Genizah manuscript C copies 18:31-33 with 19:1-3 (folio V recto), so these lines were still copied in Hebrew in the Middle Ages.
